summary.text: A tidal barrage is a dam-like wall built across a bay or river that captures energy from water moving in and out with the tides.
Sluice gates let water into the basin at high tide and release it at low tide, and turbines in the wall make power when the water level differs on each side.
Barrages carry high building costs and face opposition for changing large habitats, and few exist worldwide.

facts.label: Largest plant
facts.value: Sihwa Lake, South Korea, 254 MW, since 2011

facts.label: Long-running pioneer
facts.value: La Rance, France, 240 MW, operating since 1966

facts.label: Ancient roots
facts.value: Tide mills as early as the sixth century

facts.label: Basic parts
facts.value: Caissons, embankments, sluices, turbines and ship locks

items.prompt: An operator has filled the basin at high tide and closed the sluice gates. When should the turbines start generating?

options.label: Right away, while the tide is still high
After the sea falls enough to make a big level difference
Only once the next high tide arrives
While the basin is still being filled

items.explain: The turbine gates stay shut until the sea level falls and creates enough head across the barrage, then open to generate.

items.prompt: Why does generating power while the basin fills usually yield less than generating while it empties?

options.label: Incoming seawater is colder and slower
Turbines only spin in one direction
Ships must pass through during the flood tide
The basin's upper half holds more water than its lower half

items.explain: Ebb generation works on the upper half of the basin, which holds more water, so the level difference drops faster when generating on the flood.

items.prompt: A barrage uses electricity from the grid to pump extra water into its basin at high tide. Why would that pay off?

options.label: It cleans silt out of the basin
It keeps ships afloat at low tide
Raising the head returns much of that energy later
Pumping cools the turbines down

items.explain: Power output depends strongly on head, and water raised at high tide ends up much higher above the sea at low tide, so much of the pumping energy comes back.

items.prompt: A grid operator wants tidal power available at almost any hour, with flexible timing. Which design fits best?

options.label: A two-basin barrage
A single basin generating on the flood
A conventional river dam
A single basin with no turbines

items.explain: With two basins, one filled at high tide and one emptied at low tide, generation time is flexible and almost continuous, though the extra barrage length is costly.

items.prompt: A plan to build a barrage across an estuary promises clean power, yet local groups oppose it. What is their most likely objection?

options.label: It would make the estuary water saltier
Its turbines would be too loud for residents
It would raise local electricity prices
It would change a large ecosystem many species use

items.explain: People have opposed barrages because changing a large estuary ecosystem harms habitat for many species.

items.prompt: How does a tidal barrage handle water differently from a river dam that holds water back on one side?

options.label: It stores water for months before release
It lets water in at high tide and out at low tide
It pumps water uphill to a reservoir
It only lets water flow out to sea

items.explain: Instead of damming water on one side, a barrage lets water flow into the bay or river at high tide and releases it at low tide.
